blocks.body:
A graph on $n$ vertices (see [[graph-basics]]) has at most $\binom n2$ edges. How many can it have if it contains no triangle? Splitting the vertices into two halves and joining every vertex of one half to every vertex of the other gives about $n^2/4$ edges and no triangle, since any three vertices include two from the same half. Mantel proved in 1907 that one cannot do better.

Extremal graph theory asks this for every forbidden graph $H$: how many edges can an $n$-vertex graph have without containing $H$ as a subgraph? For complete graphs the answer is Turán's theorem. For every $H$ that is not bipartite, the Erdős–Stone theorem gives the answer up to a lower-order error, in terms of the chromatic number of $H$. For bipartite $H$ the answer is much smaller, and for many bipartite graphs, such as $K_{4,4}$ and the $8$-cycle, even its order of magnitude is unknown.

blocks.title: Extremal number
blocks.body:
For a graph $H$, the extremal number $\operatorname{ex}(n, H)$ is the largest number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices that contains no subgraph isomorphic to $H$. Graphs attaining it are called extremal graphs for $H$.

In other words, $\operatorname{ex}(n,H) + 1$ edges on $n$ vertices always force a copy of $H$, while some graph with $\operatorname{ex}(n,H)$ edges avoids it.

blocks.title: Mantel's theorem
blocks.body: Every triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices has at most $n^2/4$ edges. Hence $\operatorname{ex}(n, K_3) = \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$.

Let $x$ be a vertex of maximum degree $\Delta$, let $A$ be its set of neighbours, and let $B$ be the set of the other $n - \Delta$ vertices. No two vertices of $A$ are adjacent, because together with $x$ they would form a triangle. So every edge has at least one end in $B$, and
$$|E| \le \sum_{v \in B} \deg v \le (n - \Delta)\,\Delta \le \frac{n^2}{4},$$
the last step because $(n-\Delta)\Delta = \frac{n^2}{4} - \big(\frac n2 - \Delta\big)^2$. Since $|E|$ is an integer, $|E| \le \lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$, and the complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ and $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ is triangle-free with exactly $\lfloor n/2\rfloor\lceil n/2\rceil = \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$ edges.

blocks.title: Turán graph
blocks.body:
For $r \ge 1$, the Turán graph $T(n, r)$ is the complete $r$-partite graph on $n$ vertices whose parts have sizes as equal as possible (each $\lfloor n/r \rfloor$ or $\lceil n/r \rceil$): two vertices are adjacent exactly when they lie in different parts. Write $t(n, r)$ for its number of edges.

It contains no $K_{r+1}$, since among any $r + 1$ vertices two lie in the same part.

blocks.title: Turán's theorem (1941)
blocks.body:
For all $n, r \ge 1$, every graph on $n$ vertices without a $K_{r+1}$ has at most $t(n,r)$ edges, and $T(n,r)$ is the only such graph with exactly $t(n,r)$ edges. Moreover
$$\operatorname{ex}(n, K_{r+1}) = t(n,r) \le \Big(1 - \frac1r\Big)\frac{n^2}{2},$$
with equality in the last step exactly when $r$ divides $n$.

We prove the bound; the uniqueness of the extremal graph needs a little more care and is omitted.

Step 1: degree domination. We show by induction on $r$ that for every $K_{r+1}$-free graph $G$ there is an $r$-partite graph $H$ on the same vertex set with $\deg_H(v) \ge \deg_G(v)$ for every vertex $v$. For $r = 1$, $G$ has no edges and $H = G$ works. For $r \ge 2$, let $x$ be a vertex of maximum degree $\Delta$, $A$ its neighbourhood and $B = V \setminus A$ (which contains $x$). The graph $G[A]$ induced on $A$ contains no $K_r$, since such a clique together with $x$ would be a $K_{r+1}$. By induction there is an $(r-1)$-partite graph $H_A$ on $A$ with $\deg_{H_A}(v) \ge \deg_{G[A]}(v)$ for $v \in A$. Let $H$ consist of $H_A$ together with all edges between $A$ and $B$, and no edges inside $B$. It is $r$-partite: the $r-1$ parts of $H_A$, and $B$. For $v \in B$, $\deg_H(v) = |A| = \Delta \ge \deg_G(v)$. For $v \in A$, $\deg_H(v) = \deg_{H_A}(v) + |B| \ge \deg_{G[A]}(v) + |N_G(v) \cap B| = \deg_G(v)$.

Step 2: balancing. Summing degrees, $|E(G)| \le |E(H)|$, and $H$ has at most as many edges as the complete $r$-partite graph with the same parts, of sizes $n_1, \dots, n_r$. That graph has $\binom n2 - \sum_i \binom{n_i}{2}$ edges. If two parts have sizes $a \ge b + 2$, moving one vertex from the larger to the smaller changes $\sum_i \binom{n_i}2$ by $\binom{a-1}2 + \binom{b+1}2 - \binom a2 - \binom b2 = b - (a - 1) < 0$, so it gains edges. Repeating, the number of edges is maximised when all sizes differ by at most $1$, that is by $T(n,r)$. Hence $|E(G)| \le t(n,r)$, and $T(n,r)$ itself shows $\operatorname{ex}(n,K_{r+1}) = t(n,r)$.

Step 3: the closed-form bound. A complete $r$-partite graph with part sizes $n_i$ has $\frac12\big(n^2 - \sum n_i^2\big)$ edges. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\sum n_i^2 \ge \frac1r\big(\sum n_i\big)^2 = \frac{n^2}{r}$, with equality exactly when all $n_i$ equal $n/r$ (see [[cauchy-schwarz]]). So $t(n,r) \le \frac12\big(n^2 - \frac{n^2}{r}\big)$, with equality exactly when $r \mid n$.

blocks.title: Beyond cliques: the chromatic number decides
blocks.body:
Turán's construction generalises. If $\chi(H) = k$ (see [[graph-coloring]]), then $H$ is not a subgraph of $T(n, k-1)$, because every subgraph of $T(n, k-1)$ can be properly coloured with $k-1$ colours, one per part. So $\operatorname{ex}(n, H) \ge t(n, k-1) \approx \big(1 - \frac{1}{k-1}\big)\frac{n^2}{2}$. This simple lower bound is asymptotically correct.

Erdős–Stone theorem (Erdős and Stone 1946; in this form Erdős and Simonovits 1966). For every graph $H$ with at least one edge,
$$\operatorname{ex}(n,H) = \Big(1-\frac{1}{\chi(H)-1}+o(1)\Big)\binom n2 \qquad (n \to \infty).$$
We omit the proof. The core of it is that a graph with $(1 - \frac1r + \varepsilon)\frac{n^2}{2}$ edges, for fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ and large $n$, contains not just a $K_{r+1}$ but a complete $(r+1)$-partite graph with $t$ vertices in each part, for any fixed $t$; and every $H$ with $\chi(H) = r+1$ sits inside such a graph once $t \ge |V(H)|$.

When $H$ is bipartite, $\chi(H) = 2$ and the theorem only says $\operatorname{ex}(n,H) = o(n^2)$. That is where the subject becomes difficult.

blocks.title: Graphs without a 4-cycle
blocks.body:
Every graph on $n$ vertices that contains no cycle of length $4$ has at most
$$\frac n4\Big(1 + \sqrt{4n-3}\Big)$$
edges. In particular $\operatorname{ex}(n, C_4) \le \big(\frac12 + o(1)\big) n^{3/2}$.

Double count cherries: pairs $(v, \{a, b\})$ where $a \ne b$ are both neighbours of $v$. Counting by $v$ gives $\sum_v \binom{\deg v}{2}$. Counting by the pair $\{a, b\}$: two different vertices $v, v'$ both adjacent to $a$ and $b$ would give the $4$-cycle $a\,v\,b\,v'\,a$, so each of the $\binom n2$ pairs is counted at most once. Hence
$$\sum_v \binom{\deg v}{2} \le \binom n2.$$
Let $e$ be the number of edges and $d = 2e/n$ the average degree. By Cauchy–Schwarz $\sum_v (\deg v)^2 \ge \frac1n\big(\sum_v \deg v\big)^2 = n d^2$, so
$$\sum_v \binom{\deg v}{2} = \frac12\Big(\sum_v (\deg v)^2 - \sum_v \deg v\Big) \ge \frac n2\,(d^2 - d).$$
Combining, $\frac n2 (d^2 - d) \le \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$, so $d^2 - d - (n-1) \le 0$ and $d \le \frac{1 + \sqrt{4n-3}}{2}$. Since $e = nd/2$, this is the bound.

blocks.title: The bipartite frontier
blocks.body:
The $C_4$ bound is the right order of magnitude: graphs built from finite projective planes over a field with $q$ elements (see [[finite-fields]]) have $n = q^2 + q + 1$ vertices, no $4$-cycle, and about $\frac12 n^{3/2}$ edges, a construction due to Erdős, Rényi and Sós and to Brown (1966). So $\operatorname{ex}(n,C_4) \sim \frac12 n^{3/2}$.

A different construction links this to number theory. If $A$ is a Sidon set modulo $m$ (the sums $a + a'$ with $a, a' \in A$ are all different modulo $m$, apart from swapping $a$ and $a'$), join $x$ on one side to $y$ on the other side of a bipartite graph with sides $\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z$ whenever $x + y \in A$. A $4$-cycle $x_1 y_1 x_2 y_2$ would give $(x_1 + y_1) + (x_2 + y_2) = (y_1 + x_2) + (y_2 + x_1)$ with all four sums in $A$. By the Sidon property the pair $\{x_1+y_1, x_2+y_2\}$ equals $\{y_1+x_2, y_2+x_1\}$, which forces $x_1 = x_2$ or $y_1 = y_2$, impossible in a $4$-cycle. Dense Sidon sets (see [[sidon-sets]]) therefore give dense $C_4$-free graphs.

The same double counting gives the Kővári–Sós–Turán bound (1954): for $s \le t$, $\operatorname{ex}(n, K_{s,t}) \le c_{s,t}\, n^{2-1/s}$ for a constant $c_{s,t}$. Matching constructions are known for $s = 2$ and $s = 3$, and, by algebraic constructions of Kollár, Rónyai and Szabó and of Alon, Rónyai and Szabó, whenever $t > (s-1)!$. For $K_{4,4}$ the order of magnitude is unknown. For even cycles, Bondy and Simonovits (1974) proved $\operatorname{ex}(n, C_{2k}) = O(n^{1+1/k})$, but a matching lower bound is known only for $k = 2, 3, 5$. In this range algebraic constructions beat random ones: the [[probabilistic-method]] gives lower bounds with noticeably smaller exponents.

blocks.title: Turán numbers by hand
blocks.body: Compute $t(10, 3)$ and compare it with $\big(1 - \frac13\big)\frac{10^2}{2}$. What is the largest number of edges in a graph on $10$ vertices with no $K_4$?
blocks.solution:
The parts of $T(10,3)$ have sizes $4, 3, 3$. Edges go between different parts: $4\cdot 3 + 4 \cdot 3 + 3 \cdot 3 = 33$. Alternatively $\binom{10}{2} - \binom42 - \binom32 - \binom32 = 45 - 6 - 3 - 3 = 33$.

The closed-form bound is $\frac23 \cdot 50 = 33\tfrac13$, which is not an integer; since $3 \nmid 10$ it is not attained. By Turán's theorem the answer to the question is $t(10,3) = 33$.

blocks.title: Far-apart pairs of points
blocks.body: We are given $n$ points in the plane, all pairwise distances at most $1$. Show that at most $\lfloor n^2/3 \rfloor$ pairs of points are at distance greater than $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, and that this bound can be attained.
blocks.solution:
Let $G$ be the graph on the points whose edges are the pairs at distance greater than $1/\sqrt2$. We show that $G$ has no $K_4$.

Among any four of the points, some three $P, Q, R$ have $\angle PQR \ge 90^\circ$. If the four points are the vertices of a convex quadrilateral, its angles add up to $360^\circ$, so one is at least $90^\circ$. Otherwise one point lies inside or on the triangle formed by the other three, and the three angles at that point between pairs of the others add up to $360^\circ$, so one is at least $120^\circ$ (if three of the points are collinear, the middle one of them gives an angle of $180^\circ$). By the law of cosines, an angle of at least $90^\circ$ at $Q$ gives $PR^2 \ge PQ^2 + QR^2$. Since $PR \le 1$, we get $PQ^2 + QR^2 \le 1$, so $PQ$ or $QR$ is at most $1/\sqrt2$. Thus no four points are pairwise far apart.

By Turán's theorem with $r = 3$, $G$ has at most $t(n,3) \le \frac{n^2}{3}$ edges, hence at most $\lfloor n^2/3\rfloor$. (In fact $t(n,3) = \lfloor n^2/3 \rfloor$ for every $n$.) For a matching construction, place the points in three tiny clusters, as equal in size as possible, at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side $0.9$. Pairs in different clusters are at distance about $0.9 > 1/\sqrt2 \approx 0.707$, all distances are below $1$, and pairs in the same cluster are very close, so the far pairs are exactly the edges of $T(n,3)$.

blocks.title: Reading off asymptotics
blocks.body: Find $\operatorname{ex}(n, H)$ up to a factor $1 + o(1)$ for: (a) the octahedron $K_{2,2,2}$; (b) the Petersen graph; (c) $K_5$. What can be said about $K_{3,3}$?
blocks.solution:
(a) $K_{2,2,2}$ is complete $3$-partite, so $\chi = 3$ (it contains triangles, and the three parts give a $3$-colouring). Erdős–Stone gives $\operatorname{ex}(n, K_{2,2,2}) = (\frac12 + o(1))\binom n2 = (\frac14 + o(1))n^2$, the same leading term as for the triangle.

(b) The Petersen graph has $\chi = 3$ (see [[graph-coloring]]), so again $\operatorname{ex}(n, H) = (\frac14 + o(1)) n^2$.

(c) $\chi(K_5) = 5$, and here Turán's theorem is exact: $\operatorname{ex}(n, K_5) = t(n,4) \le \frac38 n^2$, with equality when $4 \mid n$.

For $K_{3,3}$, which is bipartite, Erdős–Stone only says $o(n^2)$. Kővári–Sós–Turán gives $O(n^{5/3})$, and this order is known to be correct, by an algebraic construction of Brown.

blocks.body:
- The formula $\big(1-\frac1r\big)\frac{n^2}{2}$ is the exact value of $\operatorname{ex}(n, K_{r+1})$ only when $r \mid n$; in general the exact value is $t(n,r)$, which is smaller.
- The Erdős–Stone theorem is asymptotic. It gives the leading term, not exact values, and for bipartite $H$ it only says $o(n^2)$.
- $\operatorname{ex}(n, H)$ is about subgraphs, not induced subgraphs. A graph contains $C_4$ even if the four vertices also span a diagonal.
- In the $C_4$ bound, count unordered pairs $\{a,b\}$ with $a \ne b$ on both sides of the double count; mixing ordered and unordered pairs gives wrong constants.

Turán-type questions run through combinatorics. In [[ramsey]] theory one colours all edges of $K_n$ and asks for a monochromatic $K_r$; Turán asks how many edges of a single colour already force one. For hypergraphs the analogue is wide open: Turán conjectured that the largest density of a $3$-uniform hypergraph without the complete $3$-graph on $4$ vertices is $5/9$ (see [[hypergraphs]]).

The bipartite case is where [[sidon-sets]] and [[finite-fields]] enter, through algebraic constructions of $C_4$-free and $K_{s,t}$-free graphs. Density results of this type, strengthened by Szemerédi's regularity lemma, lead to the removal lemma and a proof of Roth's theorem on three-term progressions (see [[arithmetic-progressions]] and [[additive-combinatorics]]). The double counting in the $C_4$ proof is the same technique as in [[pigeonhole]].

1. Show that the only triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices with $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$ edges is the complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ and $\lceil n/2 \rceil$. (Follow the equality cases in the proof of Mantel's theorem.)
2. Prove that $t(n,r) - t(n-1,r) = n - \lceil n/r \rceil$, and use it to give a proof of Turán's theorem by induction on $n$.
3. Show that a bipartite graph with $n$ vertices on each side and no $C_4$ has at most $\frac n2\big(1 + \sqrt{4n-3}\big)$ edges.
4. Use the Sidon set $\{1, 2, 4\}$ modulo $7$ to build a $C_4$-free bipartite graph with $7$ vertices on each side and $21$ edges.
